profile.research_note: [batch narration moved out of reading 2026-09-02] This is the Green Data Center, a research computing facility on Syracuse University campus in Syracuse, New York, completed in 2009 in partnership with IBM. The facility was among the first university data centers designed around on site trigeneration, using natural gas microturbines to generate electricity on site, with the resulting waste heat captured for both heating and, through absorption chillers, cooling, an approach intended to reduce reliance on the regional power grid and improve energy efficiency versus a conventional data center. The project drew industry and trade press attention at the time, including coverage in Campus Technology and Cabling Installation and Maintenance, as an early example of a university investing in sustainable data center design. Syracuse University own research computing division continues to describe the Green Data Center as central to the university high performance and research computing capacity. No specific critical IT megawattage figure was found published on the university own site. This research was carried out at the operator level in an earlier phase of this project.

reading: Syracuse University operates the Green Data Center, a research computing facility on its Syracuse, New York campus completed in 2009 in partnership with IBM. The facility was among the first university data centers designed around on site trigeneration, using natural gas microturbines to generate electricity on site, with the resulting waste heat captured for both heating and, through absorption chillers, cooling, an approach intended to reduce reliance on the regional power grid and improve overall energy efficiency compared to a conventional data center drawing all of its power from utility service. The project drew attention in industry and trade press at the time, including coverage in Campus Technology and Cabling Installation and Maintenance, as an early example of a university investing in sustainable data center design rather than treating computing infrastructure purely as a cost center. Syracuse University's own research computing division continues to describe the Green Data Center as central to the university's high performance and research computing capacity. No specific critical IT megawattage figure was found published on the university's own site during this research, so that field is left unspecified. The facility is operated by and for the university itself rather than as a commercial or colocation offering, consistent with an academic enterprise data center serving research, administrative, and instructional computing needs across the Syracuse campus.
